title: For the sake of wisdom
hookLine: all the other perfections are taught for the sake of wisdom (Bodhicaryavatara 9.1)
tomorrow: how can a table be real and not real?

cards: Ask a runner why she runs and you might hear: for the race. Why the race? To prove something.
Why prove it? Somewhere the answers run out and she laughs, because she's never asked. Plenty of things we do run on that kind of autopilot: the job, the diet, the daily habit.
They began with a reason, and then the reason quietly slipped away. Patience, effort, quiet, the exchange: that's a lot of practice. All of it for what?
Shantideva answers in the first line of his next chapter.

teach.h: TAUGHT FOR THE SAKE OF WISDOM.
teach.b: All these parts, he says, the Sage taught for the sake of wisdom. One line, and it rearranges the poem. Patience, effort, meditation, the chapters we've just walked through, aren't the destination.

They're the road. Wisdom, prajna, is where it leads: seeing things as they are. In Mahayana teaching these qualities are the paramitas, the perfections, and Shantideva says the others are taught for this one.
Why does that matter in an ordinary week?
Because practices drift when you forget what they're for. Patience can slide into putting up with anything. Effort can turn into hustle.
Quiet can become hiding. Asking for the sake of what keeps each one honest.
Some readers find this line humbling: everything so far was preparation. Others find it freeing: the hard practices were never the point by themselves; they clear the eyes.
The chapter goes on to argue for what wisdom sees; that's for the coming days. Today is only the hinge, the turn of the key. For wisdom.

how: Mahayana Buddhists study the perfections (paramitas) as a path, and the wisdom chapter of Shantideva's guide is among the texts read closely in Tibetan monastic study.

games.q: what does “for the sake of wisdom” mean?
o: wisdom is earned by studying for many long years
the other practices are all taught to lead to wisdom
only wise people should attempt these practices

games.q: the road and where it leads — tap the pairs.
p: wisdom: seeing things as they are

s: Shantideva says patience and effort are the final goal
he says the Sage taught all these parts for the sake of wisdom.
the wisdom chapter opens by saying the other parts were taught for wisdom's sake
one line, and it shows where the whole road leads.

games.q: your dad has gone to the gym for months but seems miserable about it. which question fits today's line?
o: what's it for? health, energy, time with friends? let that steer the workout.
push harder; the misery means it's working.
quit; anything that feels like a chore isn't worth doing.
games.why: Shantideva's line asks what each practice is for. when the why comes back, the practice usually changes shape.

practice: Pick one thing you practice: a habit, a sport, a prayer, a daily walk. Write its name by hand, then the words for the sake of, and finish the line with what it's really for.
If the first answer isn't the real one, ask again and write the next.

wordCard.voice: For the sake of wisdom: the opening line of Shantideva's wisdom chapter. The other practices are taught for wisdom, seeing things as they are.

orig.note: Sanskrit: wisdom, insight; in Pali, panna.

carryVoice: Keep this one: for wisdom, because every practice has a why behind it. The wisdom chapter, begun.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 9.1 (all these parts the Sage taught for the sake of wisdom)
